screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we build practical expertise for deploying shared storage in enterprise environments. You will learn why NFSv4 is the preferred Linux-native option — its single port simplicity, global namespace concept, and how Kerberos adds authentication and encryption. You will also learn how Samba implements the SMB/CIFS protocol so Linux servers can present shares to Windows clients, and why SELinux and file permissions matter for safe sharing. The lab emphasizes hands-on commands: creating the NFS pseudo-root with fsid=0, exporting directories with sec=krb5p for privacy, preparing keytabs, and configuring smb. conf, smbpasswd, and SELinux contexts for Samba. Along the way we highlight common mistakes: misconfigured fsid, clock skew that breaks Kerberos, and SELinux contexts that silently deny access. By the end you will be able to set up an NFSv4 export with Kerberos, mount it from a client persistently or on-demand, and create a Samba share accessible to specific Windows users. Think about which workloads need encrypted NFS traffic and which need Windows-compatible access; that will guide whether you choose NFSv4 or Samba for a given service.

screens.title: What is NFSv4 and why it matters
screens.narratorSegment: NFS version 4 is a major evolution of the original Network File System designed for modern networks. Its central claims are simplicity and security: it uses a single well-known port, 2049, which makes firewalls and NAT traversal easier to manage, and it exposes a single global namespace by design through the concept of a pseudo-filesystem where one export must be designated as fsid=0. Practically, that means clients mount logical paths under a single exported root instead of juggling multiple independent mount points. Security is improved not just by recommendations but by capability: NFSv4 integrates with Kerberos for authentication and can request privacy using krb5p to encrypt traffic. A concrete example is exporting /srv/nfsshare as the pseudo-root with fsid=0 and then exporting /srv/nfsshare/data to a subnet using sec=krb5p so only Kerberos-authenticated clients can read and write. Common misconceptions include thinking NFSv4 is automatically secure; it still needs Kerberos and proper export options to avoid anonymous access. Another pitfall is treating fsid=0 as optional — misplacing it breaks the namespace. Key takeaway: NFSv4 gives a cleaner namespace and stronger security primitives, but you must explicitly enable and configure them.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › NFSv4 Overview
Definition

NFSv4: single-port, global namespace, Kerberos-ready

NFSv4 simplifies firewall rules by using port 2049 and unifies exported directories under a pseudo-filesystem. It builds in security hooks to integrate with Kerberos for authentication and optional encryption.

fsid=0 (pseudo-root)
Designates the root export for the NFSv4 pseudo-filesystem; all other exports must be subdirectories.
sec=krb5p
Kerberos privacy mode: authentication, integrity, and encryption for NFS traffic.
Key Takeaway

NFSv4 provides a cleaner namespace and stronger security primitives, but they must be intentionally configured.

Concrete Example
# /etc/exports example /srv/nfsshare *(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,fsid=0) /srv/nfsshare/data 192.168.10.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,sec=krb5p)
Misconception

Assuming NFSv4 is secure out-of-the-box. Without Kerberos and correct export options you can still allow unauthenticated or overly permissive access.

Check

Run showmount -e server to confirm the pseudo-root and subexports are visible as intended.

screens.title: Preparing /etc/exports and fsid=0
screens.narratorSegment: The /etc/exports file declares what the NFS server will export and which clients may mount those directories. For NFSv4 you must declare a global export that becomes the pseudo-root by using fsid=0. If you forget fsid=0 or export directories outside that tree, clients will experience inconsistent mount paths. A recommended pattern is to make /srv/nfsshare the fsid=0 export, then export subdirectories beneath it with network restrictions and security options. For security, prefer explicit subnet restrictions rather than a wildcard, enable sync to ensure writes are committed, and use sec=krb5p when Kerberos is available. A concrete export example is shown in the visual: the pseudo-root line with fsid=0 and a /data sub-export limited to 192.168.10.0/24 using krb5p. After editing /etc/exports, always run exportfs -rv to refresh the kernel export table and check visibility with showmount -e. Misconfigurations often come from using no_subtree_check incorrectly or forgetting to restrict exports; the quick remediation path is to review /etc/exports syntax, re-export, and inspect server logs. Preparing /etc/exports and fsid=0 means designate a single fsid=0 export, place other exports as subdirectories, restrict by subnet, and prefer sec=krb5p for privacy.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › /etc/exports & fsid=0
Process

Declare pseudo-root, then subexports

  1. Create /srv/nfsshare and set permissive root permissions for the root export.
  2. Add fsid=0 line to /etc/exports to mark the pseudo-root.
  3. Add subdirectory exports under that tree with subnet restrictions and sec=krb5p where needed.
  4. Run exportfs -rv and verify showmount -e.
Key Takeaway

fsid=0 centralizes the NFSv4 namespace; every other export must be a subdirectory of that root.

Example
# /etc/exports
/srv/nfsshare *(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,fsid=0)
/srv/nfsshare/data 192.168.10.0/24(rw,sync,no_subtree_check,sec=krb5p)
Common mistakes
  • Placing fsid=0 on a non-root export or omitting it entirely.
  • Using wildcards for exports that should be subnet-limited.
  • Neglecting to run exportfs after editing exports.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.8 › NFS Server Setup
Checklist
  1. Install utilities: sudo dnf install nfs-utils krb5-workstation -y
  2. Create directories and set ownership/permissions
  3. Edit /etc/exports and mark fsid=0
  4. Run sudo exportfs -rv to refresh exports
  5. Enable and start services: sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-server rpcbind
  6. Open firewall: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=nfs; firewall-cmd --reload
Pro tip

Keep the pseudo-root and data directories separated so permissions can be stricter on data while root remains stable for mounts.

Commands (starter)
sudo dnf install nfs-utils krb5-workstation -y
sudo mkdir -p /srv/nfsshare/data
sudo chmod 0755 /srv/nfsshare
sudo chmod 0770 /srv/nfsshare/data
sudo exportfs -rv
sudo systemctl enable --now nfs-server rpcbind
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=nfs
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Common mistake

Starting only nfs-server without rpcbind or rpc-gssd (for Kerberos) will produce incomplete service registration and failing mounts.

screens.title: Kerberos authentication for NFSv4
screens.narratorSegment: Kerberos is the recommended authentication mechanism for secure NFSv4 deployments. At a high level, Kerberos provides strong mutual authentication using a central Key Distribution Center. For NFS, a service principal such as nfs/server. example. com@REALM. COM must be created in the KDC and its key material stored in a keytab on the NFS server. The server uses rpc-gssd to accept and verify client Kerberos tickets. On the client side, users obtain tickets using kinit, and mounts use options like sec=krb5p to require privacy. A concrete example: after creating the service principal on the KDC and adding it to /etc/krb5. keytab, run klist -kt to verify the keytab contains the nfs principal. Enable rpc-gssd with systemctl enable --now rpc-gssd. A frequent failure mode is clock skew; Kerberos will reject tickets if server, client, and KDC clocks are out of sync. Troubleshoot by confirming chronyd or ntpd is running on all hosts and using klist -s or kinit to test ticket acquisition. Key takeaway: Kerberos adds critical authentication and with krb5p provides encryption, but it requires correct principals, keytabs, services, and time synchronization to work reliably.

Architecture

KDC, NFS server, and clients

KDC
Hosts service principals and issues tickets used for authentication.

# copy to server and secure permissions

Kerberos requires principals, a secure keytab, rpc-gssd, and synchronized clocks to function reliably with NFSv4.

screens.narratorSegment: Mounting an NFSv4 export on a client is straightforward when services and Kerberos are in place. After installing nfs-utils and krb5-workstation on the client, a user or service must obtain a Kerberos ticket using kinit clientuser@REALM. COM before attempting a krb5p mount. The mount command uses type nfs4 and options including sec=krb5p to indicate privacy. For example, mount -t nfs4 -o sec=krb5p server. example. com:/data /mnt/nfs_data will mount a subdirectory exported beneath the pseudo-root. To make mounts persistent across reboots add an /etc/fstab entry with nfs4, sec=krb5p, and _netdev so the system waits for network initialization. For many environments autofs is preferable: it performs on-demand mounts, reducing connection overhead and avoiding failed mounts at boot when network services aren't ready. A common misconception is to place plain nfs mounts in fstab without _netdev, causing slow boot or failed mounts; another is omitting a kinit step when using Kerberos, which leads to permission denied. Always verify the mount with mount or showmount and test file read/write ownership to confirm the Kerberos identity maps correctly on the server. screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting NFS in production is largely about methodical checks. Start with visibility: showmount -e server will tell you whether the server is exporting what you expect. If the export is present but mounts fail with permission denied when using sec=krb5p, check two Kerberos staples: time synchronization and keytab validity. Use date and chronyc tracking to confirm clocks are within tolerance; then run klist -kt /etc/krb5. keytab on the server to ensure the nfs principal is present. Another frequent mistake is misconfigured fsid=0 — if subexports are not nested under the pseudo-root they will not be presented correctly. Use journalctl -u nfs-server and /var/log/messages to find server-side errors and nfsstat -c on clients to see RPC errors. screens.title: CIFS/SMB and Samba basics
screens.narratorSegment: Samba is the open-source suite that implements the SMB/CIFS protocols so Linux and Unix systems can offer file and print services to Windows clients. Samba's core configuration lives in /etc/samba/smb. conf where you define shares, workgroup settings, and security modes. Samba can operate in user-level security where smbpasswd manages a Samba-specific password database, allowing control of which Linux accounts can access shares. A typical share definition includes path, valid users, create and directory masks, and browseable/writable flags. For Windows interoperability you must consider both filesystem permissions and Samba-level restrictions; a file may be blocked by the OS-level permissions or by Samba’s valid users list. SELinux also influences access, because the kernel enforces SELinux labels irrespective of Samba settings. A concrete example is a share named windows_data pointing to /srv/sambashare with valid users set to smbuser. A common misconception is that changing smb. conf alone makes a share accessible; in practice you also need to create the smbuser, set samba passwords with smbpasswd, and apply correct filesystem ownership and SELinux context. The closing takeaway: Samba bridges protocols but requires coordinated configuration at the OS, Samba, and SELinux layers.

screens.narratorSegment: Configuring Samba for a production share requires careful coordination between the Samba configuration, underlying filesystem permissions, and Samba's own password database. Start by installing Samba and creating the directory to share, for example /srv/sambashare. Set filesystem permissions and group ownership so only intended users can access the files. In smb. conf under the [global] section set workgroup and security=user; define the share with path, valid users, create and directory masks. Enable and start smb and nmb services, and open the samba service in the firewall. After changes, use testparm to validate the configuration and smbstatus to monitor active sessions. A common mistake is creating the share but forgetting to add the user to smbpasswd or to the local group, which results in access denied on connection attempts. screens.title: SELinux and Samba — common denials and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux enforces Mandatory Access Control that applies equally to Samba. Even with correct filesystem ownership and a valid Samba user, SELinux can block access if the shared directory lacks the samba_share_t context. The typical symptom is access denied on Windows clients while local operations by root succeed. To diagnose SELinux denials inspect audit messages using ausearch for AVC denials or run sealert to get a summarized analysis. The remediation is to label the directory with semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t "/srv/sambashare(/.*)?" and then apply restorecon -Rv to relabel files. Additionally, certain boolean settings such as samba_enable_home_dirs or samba_export_all_rw may be required depending on your sharing pattern; set them with setsebool -P. A common misconception is to disable SELinux to make Samba work; instead, prefer correct labeling and booleans because SELinux provides important confinement. After relabeling restart Samba services and test access. Key takeaway: SELinux denials frequently masquerade as Samba misconfigurations; use the audit logs to confirm and then relabel safely rather than disabling SELinux. Windows clients receive Access Denied while Samba and filesystem permissions appear correct. This often indicates SELinux blocking access.

Disabling SELinux fixes symptoms but removes valuable security controls. Relabel and set booleans instead.

screens.narratorSegment: When Windows clients cannot connect to a Samba share, follow a layered verification approach. First check smb. conf syntax with testparm; a syntax error can prevent Samba from loading a share definition. Next, examine active sessions with smbstatus to see whether the client ever authenticates and to inspect file locks. If authentication fails, confirm the user exists in both the system and Samba password database and that smbpasswd -a was run. If access is denied despite valid users, audit SELinux denials as described previously; if SELinux is clear, inspect filesystem ownership and group membership. Firewall rules can also obstruct SMB; ensure the samba service is permitted through firewall-cmd. Logs in /var/log/samba/ are valuable: they show authentication attempts and service errors. A specific common mistake is relying on POSIX permissions only; Samba enforces both POSIX and share-level restrictions, so both must allow access. For verification, connect from a Windows client or a Linux CIFS client and test read/write operations, then review smbstatus and smb logs to correlate the client's UID/GID mapping with expected outcomes. Closing question: after testparm and smbstatus, where would you check next to confirm SELinux isn't blocking the share?

screens.title: When to choose NFSv4 vs Samba
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between NFSv4 and Samba depends on client mix, feature needs, and security requirements. If your environment is primarily Linux and you need POSIX semantics, performance, and a Linux-friendly access model, NFSv4 is usually the better fit. It integrates naturally with Unix permissions and offers Kerberos integration for strong authentication and privacy. If you must support Windows clients with native SMB semantics, ACLs, and printer sharing, Samba is necessary because Windows clients expect SMB/CIFS. Another consideration is namespace and mount behavior: NFS exposes POSIX filesystems mounted into the client kernel namespace, while Samba provides network shares that Windows maps as network drives. Security choices differ: NFSv4 benefits from Kerberos and a single port, while Samba requires careful SELinux labeling and user-level password management. A practical example: host home directories for Linux-only developers — use NFSv4 with Kerberos; share a corporate documents folder accessible from Windows desktops — use Samba and ensure samba_share_t labeling. Misconception: assuming one protocol supersedes the other; in enterprise you often run both, each where it best fits. NFS version 4 is a major evolution of the original Network File System designed for modern networks. Its central claims are simplicity and security: it uses a single well-known port, 2049, which makes firewalls and NAT traversal easier to manage, and it exposes a single global namespace by design through the concept of a pseudo-filesystem where one export must be designated as fsid=0. Practically, that means clients mount logical paths under a single exported root instead of juggling multiple independent mount points. Security is improved not just by recommendations but by capability: NFSv4 integrates with Kerberos for authentication and can request privacy using krb5p to encrypt traffic. A concrete example is exporting /srv/nfsshare as the pseudo-root with fsid=0 and then exporting /srv/nfsshare/data to a subnet using sec=krb5p so only Kerberos-authenticated clients can read and write. Common misconceptions include thinking NFSv4 is automatically secure; it still needs Kerberos and proper export options to avoid anonymous access. Another pitfall is treating fsid=0 as optional — misplacing it breaks the namespace. Key takeaway: NFSv4 gives a cleaner namespace and stronger security primitives, but you must explicitly enable and configure them.

The /etc/exports file declares what the NFS server will export and which clients may mount those directories. For NFSv4 you must declare a global export that becomes the pseudo-root by using fsid=0. If you forget fsid=0 or export directories outside that tree, clients will experience inconsistent mount paths. A recommended pattern is to make /srv/nfsshare the fsid=0 export, then export subdirectories beneath it with network restrictions and security options. For security, prefer explicit subnet restrictions rather than a wildcard, enable sync to ensure writes are committed, and use sec=krb5p when Kerberos is available. After editing /etc/exports, always run exportfs -rv to refresh the kernel export table and check visibility with showmount -e. Misconfigurations often come from using no_subtree_check incorrectly or forgetting to restrict exports; the quick remediation path is to review /etc/exports syntax, re-export, and inspect server logs. Preparing /etc/exports and fsid=0 means designate a single fsid=0 export, place other exports as subdirectories, restrict by subnet, and prefer sec=krb5p for privacy.. Kerberos is the recommended authentication mechanism for secure NFSv4 deployments. At a high level, Kerberos provides strong mutual authentication using a central Key Distribution Center. For NFS, a service principal such as nfs/server. example. com@REALM. COM must be created in the KDC and its key material stored in a keytab on the NFS server. The server uses rpc-gssd to accept and verify client Kerberos tickets. On the client side, users obtain tickets using kinit, and mounts use options like sec=krb5p to require privacy. A concrete example: after creating the service principal on the KDC and adding it to /etc/krb5. keytab, run klist -kt to verify the keytab contains the nfs principal. Enable rpc-gssd with systemctl enable --now rpc-gssd. A frequent failure mode is clock skew; Kerberos will reject tickets if server, client, and KDC clocks are out of sync. Troubleshoot by confirming chronyd or ntpd is running on all hosts and using klist -s or kinit to test ticket acquisition. Key takeaway: Kerberos adds critical authentication and with krb5p provides encryption, but it requires correct principals, keytabs, services, and time synchronization to work reliably.

Mounting an NFSv4 export on a client is straightforward when services and Kerberos are in place. After installing nfs-utils and krb5-workstation on the client, a user or service must obtain a Kerberos ticket using kinit clientuser@REALM. COM before attempting a krb5p mount. The mount command uses type nfs4 and options including sec=krb5p to indicate privacy. For example, mount -t nfs4 -o sec=krb5p server. example. com:/data /mnt/nfs_data will mount a subdirectory exported beneath the pseudo-root. To make mounts persistent across reboots add an /etc/fstab entry with nfs4, sec=krb5p, and _netdev so the system waits for network initialization. For many environments autofs is preferable: it performs on-demand mounts, reducing connection overhead and avoiding failed mounts at boot when network services aren't ready. A common misconception is to place plain nfs mounts in fstab without _netdev, causing slow boot or failed mounts; another is omitting a kinit step when using Kerberos, which leads to permission denied. Always verify the mount with mount or showmount and test file read/write ownership to confirm the Kerberos identity maps correctly on the server. Troubleshooting NFS in production is largely about methodical checks. Start with visibility: showmount -e server will tell you whether the server is exporting what you expect. If the export is present but mounts fail with permission denied when using sec=krb5p, check two Kerberos staples: time synchronization and keytab validity. Use date and chronyc tracking to confirm clocks are within tolerance; then run klist -kt /etc/krb5. keytab on the server to ensure the nfs principal is present. If mounts fail with permission or ownership oddities, inspect filesystem permissions on the server side and remember that NFS maps unknown UIDs to nobody by default unless id mapping is used. Firewall-related failures often arise when non-2049 ports are still required by older NFS versions; with NFSv4 the single port simplifies this but ensure the nfs service is allowed in firewall-cmd. Another frequent mistake is misconfigured fsid=0 — if subexports are not nested under the pseudo-root they will not be presented correctly. Use journalctl -u nfs-server and /var/log/messages to find server-side errors and nfsstat -c on clients to see RPC errors. Samba is the open-source suite that implements the SMB/CIFS protocols so Linux and Unix systems can offer file and print services to Windows clients. Samba's core configuration lives in /etc/samba/smb. conf where you define shares, workgroup settings, and security modes. Samba can operate in user-level security where smbpasswd manages a Samba-specific password database, allowing control of which Linux accounts can access shares. A typical share definition includes path, valid users, create and directory masks, and browseable/writable flags. For Windows interoperability you must consider both filesystem permissions and Samba-level restrictions; a file may be blocked by the OS-level permissions or by Samba’s valid users list. SELinux also influences access, because the kernel enforces SELinux labels irrespective of Samba settings. A concrete example is a share named windows_data pointing to /srv/sambashare with valid users set to smbuser. A common misconception is that changing smb. conf alone makes a share accessible; in practice you also need to create the smbuser, set samba passwords with smbpasswd, and apply correct filesystem ownership and SELinux context. The closing takeaway: Samba bridges protocols but requires coordinated configuration at the OS, Samba, and SELinux layers.

Configuring Samba for a production share requires careful coordination between the Samba configuration, underlying filesystem permissions, and Samba's own password database. Start by installing Samba and creating the directory to share, for example /srv/sambashare. Set filesystem permissions and group ownership so only intended users can access the files. In smb. conf under the [global] section set workgroup and security=user; define the share with path, valid users, create and directory masks. Samba stores credentials separately, so create a system user (with no login shell) and add them to the Samba group, then run smbpasswd -a smbuser to add the user to Samba’s password database. Enable and start smb and nmb services, and open the samba service in the firewall. After changes, use testparm to validate the configuration and smbstatus to monitor active sessions. A common mistake is creating the share but forgetting to add the user to smbpasswd or to the local group, which results in access denied on connection attempts. Key takeaway: think in layers — filesystem permissions, Samba user database, and SELinux labeling must all permit access. SELinux enforces Mandatory Access Control that applies equally to Samba. Even with correct filesystem ownership and a valid Samba user, SELinux can block access if the shared directory lacks the samba_share_t context. The typical symptom is access denied on Windows clients while local operations by root succeed. To diagnose SELinux denials inspect audit messages using ausearch for AVC denials or run sealert to get a summarized analysis. The remediation is to label the directory with semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t "/srv/sambashare(/.*)?" and then apply restorecon -Rv to relabel files. Additionally, certain boolean settings such as samba_enable_home_dirs or samba_export_all_rw may be required depending on your sharing pattern; set them with setsebool -P. A common misconception is to disable SELinux to make Samba work; instead, prefer correct labeling and booleans because SELinux provides important confinement. After relabeling restart Samba services and test access. Key takeaway: SELinux denials frequently masquerade as Samba misconfigurations; use the audit logs to confirm and then relabel safely rather than disabling SELinux. When Windows clients cannot connect to a Samba share, follow a layered verification approach. First check smb. conf syntax with testparm; a syntax error can prevent Samba from loading a share definition. Next, examine active sessions with smbstatus to see whether the client ever authenticates and to inspect file locks. If authentication fails, confirm the user exists in both the system and Samba password database and that smbpasswd -a was run. If access is denied despite valid users, audit SELinux denials as described previously; if SELinux is clear, inspect filesystem ownership and group membership. Firewall rules can also obstruct SMB; ensure the samba service is permitted through firewall-cmd. Logs in /var/log/samba/ are valuable: they show authentication attempts and service errors. A specific common mistake is relying on POSIX permissions only; Samba enforces both POSIX and share-level restrictions, so both must allow access. For verification, connect from a Windows client or a Linux CIFS client and test read/write operations, then review smbstatus and smb logs to correlate the client's UID/GID mapping with expected outcomes. Choosing between NFSv4 and Samba depends on client mix, feature needs, and security requirements. If your environment is primarily Linux and you need POSIX semantics, performance, and a Linux-friendly access model, NFSv4 is usually the better fit. It integrates naturally with Unix permissions and offers Kerberos integration for strong authentication and privacy. If you must support Windows clients with native SMB semantics, ACLs, and printer sharing, Samba is necessary because Windows clients expect SMB/CIFS. Another consideration is namespace and mount behavior: NFS exposes POSIX filesystems mounted into the client kernel namespace, while Samba provides network shares that Windows maps as network drives. Security choices differ: NFSv4 benefits from Kerberos and a single port, while Samba requires careful SELinux labeling and user-level password management. A practical example: host home directories for Linux-only developers — use NFSv4 with Kerberos; share a corporate documents folder accessible from Windows desktops — use Samba and ensure samba_share_t labeling. Misconception: assuming one protocol supersedes the other; in enterprise you often run both, each where it best fits.
